picks.style: late antique latin prayer-hymn, unaccompanied plainchant with soft drone, low male voice, slow, reverent, sparse
picks.why: A complete morning prayer — 'let no day be passed by me in sadness' — self-contained and quietly devastating.

picks.style: late roman elegiac song, cithara and low strings, warm tenor, building anaphora, yearning, rubato
picks.why: The 'now he leaves Spain, now he approaches, now he beats at thy door' build is pure refrain, ending on a heartbreak.

picks.style: latin rhetorical lament, lyre and frame drum, declamatory male voice, insistent, gathering, measured
picks.why: 'Nature made nothing dumb' — a whole catalogue of the world's noises marshalled against one friend's silence.

picks.style: mock funeral dirge, roman satire, low brass and reedy flutes, ironic massed chorus, processional, slow and swaggering
picks.why: A parody lament with real dirge shape — 'Mourn, mourn, pettifoggers, ye venal crew' is a made refrain.

picks.style: sardonic latin cabaret, plucked lyre and hand percussion, dry male voice, jaunty, looping, unresolved
picks.why: The bottomless dice-box is the sharpest image in the satire and the verse already circles like the punishment.

picks.style: classical spinning-song, kithara and light strings, bright interlacing female voices, lilting, incantatory
picks.why: The Fates pulling golden thread while Phoebus plays — a genuine lyric interlude in a prose satire.

picks.style: ancient greek comic chorus, aulos and lyre, frame drum, layered voices with birdcall syllables, lively, dancing
picks.why: The swan chorus on the Hebrus with its tiotiotiotinx refrain — the play's one true song, already built to be sung.

picks.style: mock dithyramb, aulos and shimmering strings, high wavering male voice, floating, airy, absurdly grand
picks.why: 'Give me wings and I will fly into the topmost airs to gather fresh songs in the clouds' — the line the play is remembered by.

picks.style: english pastoral elegy, harpsichord and recorder, plaintive soprano, strophic, grieving, unhurried
picks.why: The goldfinch's lament built on a hammering 'Was it for this' — refrain, grief, and concrete nest-making detail.

picks.style: georgian pastoral air, baroque guitar and flute, warm tenor, courting, lilting, springlike
picks.why: The blackbird's wooing song — 'the wintry storms are flown, and gentle Zephyrs fan the air' — a clean, singable love lyric.

picks.style: english georgian hymn-air, chamber organ and viola, reflective tenor, slow, valedictory
picks.why: 'To-morrow on my roof your guests no more' turns departing swallows into a whole theory of mortality in four lines.

picks.style: english broadside ballad, fiddle and hurdy-gurdy, comic male-female duet, bouncing, nonsense refrain, brisk
picks.why: Roger tapping at Dolly's window with thumpaty-thump — the nonsense refrain is already a hook.

picks.style: georgian ballad-opera air, harpsichord and violin, plain sincere tenor, tender, strophic with refrain
picks.why: Sally of our Alley — the refrain repeats, the devotion is comic and real, and it was written to be sung.

picks.style: london street ballad, fiddle and tabor, bright saucy female voice, brisk, defiant, strophic
picks.why: Sally's answering ballad gives the woman the voice and the same 'in spite of all our Alley' refrain.

picks.style: georgian drawing-room song, harpsichord and cello, wry baritone, elegant, moderate, lightly mocking
picks.why: 'To die's a lesson we shall know too soon without a master' — a complete, epigrammatic argument against sermons on death.

picks.style: restoration catch, lute and viol, sly tenor, light, teasing, dance-like
picks.why: The Chloe song is a whole seduction argument in four neat stanzas, blasphemous and self-contained.

picks.style: ancient greek philosophical chant, lyre and low drone, grave male voice, slow, declamatory, austere
picks.why: Carries the Sophoclean quatrain — 'neither now nor yesterday these deep conceits of God began' — the best line available in this work.

picks.style: greek gnomic verse, kithara and hand drum, stern male voice, measured, oracular, sparse
picks.why: Only candidate, but a real gnomic couplet: the man who plots his neighbour's harm plots it against his own heart.
